status: Wired into the builder in round 43 (apply_laundered_r39 reads measured_buyers; decisions: quadrature ranges, flat expected path, Malta's bunker rule kept, Urals band dropped for measured series). The 'buyers' block holds the research-stage estimates (variants); the built values are in laundered_r43-notes.md, 'Wired in'.
units: EUR bn nominal unless stated (USD at the ECB yearly averages laundered_r39.json uses; AUD at ECB monthly averages: 2019 1.6106, 2020 1.6554, 2021 1.5747, 2022 1.5174, 2023 1.6285, 2024 1.6399, 2025 1.7514, 2026 Jan-Sep 1.6507). 2026 = January-August, not annualised. 'Levels' are the money Russia was paid for the crude inside the fuel a country bought (laund.years in site/data.json). Laundered part = the site's 'laund' part (calc() delta3 at Russia's net gain), cumulative 2022-2026, positive = Russia lost (credit to the buyer), worked out with the site's own model (site/index.html calc(), pSignMC) on patched copies of site/data.json of 2026-10-24.
question: Narrow the laundered-oil part for the countries where it decides certainty (Cyprus, Malta, the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Chile; Fiji and South Africa on Russia's earnings; also Australia, New Zealand, Pakistan): which inputs make the range wide, and what better data say.
key_findings: Cyprus: Eurostat's energy statistics (imports by country of last consignment) show Cyprus's own supply of 2.3-2.5 Mt a year came from Greece, Israel, Spain and Italy; Türkiye 0-44 kt, 'not specified' 0-37 kt. The Comext 'not specified extra-EU' imports (QW, 1.1 Mt in 2024, 1.6 Mt in 2025) that laundered_eu.json counted 40% (10-80%) Turkish/Indian-refined are not in that supply: Cyprus re-exported 1.5-3.7 Mt of fuel a year in 2023-2025 (Libya, Lebanon, Egypt, Nigeria). Cyprus's own fuel from Russian crude therefore fell after the EU bans (Greek, Italian, Belgian and Dutch refiners ran 10-32% Russian crude in 2019-2021, 0 from 2023): the laundered part changes sign, from -0.19 bn (-0.97 to +0.23) to +0.24 bn (+0.07 to +0.34; stacked ends -0.04 to +0.40).

Malta: 80% of its oil supply is international maritime bunkers (Eurostat INTMARB/imports 0.80 in 2022-2024; energy2.json's 0.81 confirmed); inland use is 17-19%. Its supply came from Italy, Spain, Greece, Croatia, Algeria, Israel and Caspian ports; Türkiye 60-73 kt a year, against CREA-implied ~0.2 Mt. Recomputed by consignor, the part is +0.07 bn (-0.03 to +0.12) under the current half-bunker rule, or +0.02 (0.00 to +0.03) if only inland use is charged (bunkers to no country, as the method page says).

Chile: the width is an artefact of the 'OTHER' 2% high share applied to US-refined fuel (75-85% of Chile's imports). EIA: US imports from Russia were 673 kb/d in 2021 (4.4% of refinery crude input at most), 147 in 2022 and 0 from 2023; under option A, US refiners (not netted) pass nothing on, as Korea and Japan. With US at zero the range shrinks to a fifth and stays positive.

Philippines and Pakistan: the largest single driver is not data but the expected path (bmul keeps the old China-route pre-war growth, x1.25-1.8 by 2026 in the middle case). The r39 docstring says the measured buyers' pre-war level is flat; with a flat path (no-war price only, +-15%) the Philippines' laundered credit nearly vanishes (+0.04 bn instead of +0.64) and its net falls to 89% chance. Owner decision.

India's Russian share in 2026 is higher than r39's 0.30: India's monthly customs (UN Comtrade) give 20.6% in January rising to 53.7% in July (Jan-Jul 37.5%), CREA 55.5% in July: Jan-Aug about 0.39 (0.29-0.47).

Türkiye: EPDK's annual oil market reports give the Russian share of crude imports as 33.6% (2019), 11.1%, 17.3%, 35.8%, 34.1%, 56.4%, 47.7% (2025) and 26.9% for Jan-Aug 2026 (turkey_gas_r43.json, same reports); r39 used 0.20 for 2019 and 0.45 for 2026.

EU refiners differ: Eurostat crude imports from Russia in 2019-2021 were Greece 10-18%, Spain 2-5%, Italy 10-14%, France 9-13%, Netherlands 27-32%, Belgium 29-32%, Finland 83-92%, Lithuania 73-80%, Poland 63-72%; r39 used one EU share of 27%. Pre-war charges for buyers of Italian, Spanish and Greek fuel (South Africa, Cyprus, Malta, Chile) fall.

Australia: APS (monthly, by source country, to August 2026) replaces CREA-based values. It confirms CREA's order of magnitude (2025 Russian crude in fuel 1.27 bn against CREA's 1.6 bn of fuel 'made from Russian crude' Feb 2025-Jan 2026, about 1.1 bn of crude) but raises the pre-war level (Chinese fuel at China's 15.5% Russian crude), so the part hardly moves (-1.58 bn).

Range construction: r39 stacks the low (and high) ends of quantity, origin share and crude content, and the site then adds the Urals price band in calc(), which partly re-counts the price inside crude content. Combining the independent factors in quadrature (as calc() does for every part's own terms) is what moves the Philippines, Papua New Guinea and New Zealand; data alone (stacked ends kept) moves Chile, Cyprus, Malta and Fiji.

origin_russian_share_r43.note: (central, low, high) Russian share of the origin's crude (or of a hub's pool), option A as in r39 (refiners not netted here at zero). India: UN Comtrade (India's own customs, tonnes) 2019-2025, 2026 from India's monthly customs Jan-Jul plus CREA July; band from the exporting refineries' deviation (KSE: six exporting refineries' Russian-derived exports 48%/27%/21% against national ~35/30/33% in three periods 2025-26). Türkiye: EPDK. EU members: Eurostat nrg_ti_oil crude imports from Russia / total (2025-2026 = 2024). USA: 0 (EIA; option A). China, UAE, Brunei, Korea, Japan, Thailand: unchanged from laundered_r39.json. Hub pools: r39's pools rescaled by the new shares of their product imports' origins, band x0.8-1.25.

cyprus_malta_bunkers.how_the_site_counts_it: Method page: bunkers have no buyer country and stay with the hub. Builder: Malta keeps 1 - 0.5 x 0.81 = 0.595 of its laundered oil in the middle case (HUB_BUNKER_HALF_MID, judgement), all of it at the high end, none of the bunker share at the low end; Cyprus is not a hub (all charged). The data: Cyprus's imports are 88-93% inland use, Malta's 17-20%. Cyprus is a trading hub too (re-exports), but of fuel that does not enter its energy supply.
